title: BAR U2·W2 — Public-Company & SEC Reporting (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — reporting to the public markets

A company that sells securities to the public enters the SEC's reporting regime, and BAR tests its mechanics: the required filings, the diluted EPS the market watches, segment and interim disclosures, and the controls regime under Sarbanes-Oxley. MBG is privately held, but understanding public reporting is squarely on the BAR blueprint and rounds out the technical-reporting area.

The SEC filing framework

Public companies file on prescribed forms. The 10-K is the audited annual report (financial statements, MD&A, risk factors, controls); the 10-Q is the quarterly report (reviewed, not audited); and the 8-K reports material events between periodic reports (an acquisition, a change of auditor, a bankruptcy) within four business days. A proxy statement supports shareholder votes, an S-1 registers a new securities offering, and insiders file Forms 3, 4, and 5 for their holdings and trades. Filing deadlines vary by filer status (large accelerated, accelerated, non-accelerated).

MD&A and the annual report

Management's Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) is the narrative bridge between the numbers and the business — management's explanation of results, liquidity and capital resources, known trends and uncertainties, and critical accounting estimates. It is required but unaudited (the auditor reads it for material inconsistency, as in AUD Unit 2). Together with the audited statements, the risk factors, and the controls report, MD&A makes the 10-K the central document a public-company analyst reads.

Diluted earnings per share

The public-company metric is EPS. Basic EPS = (net income − preferred dividends) ÷ weighted-average common shares. Diluted EPS adds the dilutive effect of options/warrants (the treasury-stock method) and convertibles (the if-converted method). Worked example: net income available to common of $900,000 over 300,000 weighted shares is $3.00 basic; if 30,000 options with a $20 exercise price exist while the average market price is $25, the treasury-stock method adds 6,000 net shares ($600,000 of proceeds buys back 24,000 shares), so diluted EPS = $900,000 ÷ 306,000 = $2.94. Only dilutive securities are included; antidilutive ones are ignored, so diluted EPS is always less than or equal to basic.

Segment and interim reporting

Public companies disclose operating segments under the management approach (ASC 280) — any segment meeting a 10% test of revenue, profit/loss, or assets is reportable, with reported segments covering at least 75% of external revenue, plus entity-wide disclosures (products, geography, major customers). Interim reports (ASC 270) treat each period as an integral part of the year — income taxes use the estimated annual effective rate — while recognizing some items discretely (a permanent inventory write-down). Both give investors visibility the annual aggregate hides.

Related parties, subsequent events, and uncertainties

Three disclosure areas protect investors. Related-party transactions must be disclosed (the nature of the relationship, the amounts, and terms) because arm's-length cannot be presumed. Subsequent events are recognized (Type I) or disclosed (Type II) per the FAR rules, through the date the statements are issued. Risks and uncertainties — significant estimates, concentrations (a major customer or supplier), and vulnerabilities — are disclosed so users can assess what could change. These narrative disclosures are as exam-relevant as the numbers.

Non-GAAP measures and XBRL

Companies often present non-GAAP measures (adjusted EBITDA, free cash flow) to tell their story, but Regulation G requires the most comparable GAAP measure with a reconciliation, and the non-GAAP figure may not be more prominent or misleading. Filings are tagged in XBRL (eXtensible Business Reporting Language), machine-readable tags that let regulators and analysts extract and compare data automatically. Both reflect the SEC's push for transparency and comparability in how results are communicated.

Sarbanes-Oxley and internal control

Sarbanes-Oxley reshaped public-company reporting. §302 requires the CEO and CFO to certify the financial statements and disclosure controls; §404 requires management to assess internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) and, for accelerated and large accelerated filers, the external auditor to attest to it (the integrated audit and CAMs from AUD Unit 2). SOX also created the PCAOB to oversee auditors, mandated audit-committee independence, and restricted auditor non-audit services. The controls regime is the structural backbone behind the reliability the SEC filings promise.

Registration, exemptions, and comprehensive income

Going public starts with registration under the Securities Act of 1933 (the S-1 and prospectus), unless an exemption applies — the most common being Regulation D private placements to accredited investors. Ongoing reporting then follows under the 1934 Act. Public statements also present comprehensive income — net income plus other comprehensive income (OCI) — in a single statement or two consecutive statements; OCI collects the AFS, hedge, pension, and foreign-currency items routed around net income in earlier FAR units, with a reclassification adjustment when they are realized. Reporting discontinued operations (a disposed component representing a strategic shift) separately, net of tax, and presenting earnings per share for income from continuing operations and for net income, complete the income-statement presentation the SEC expects.

Filer status, deadlines, and the audit committee

A company's filer status — large accelerated, accelerated, or non-accelerated — sets its filing deadlines and whether the §404(b) auditor ICFR attestation applies (only accelerated and large accelerated filers). The audit committee, composed of independent directors, hires and oversees the external auditor, pre-approves services, and handles whistleblower complaints — a Sarbanes-Oxley governance requirement. These structural rules, with the certification and ICFR requirements, are why public reporting carries a credibility a private company's statements achieve only through a voluntary audit.

Required statements and the going-concern note

A complete set of public financial statements includes the balance sheet, income statement (with continuing operations, discontinued operations, and EPS), statement of comprehensive income, statement of cash flows, statement of changes in stockholders' equity, and the notes. Management must also evaluate and, where substantial doubt exists, disclose going-concern uncertainty, on which the auditor reports (AUD Unit 2). The summary of significant accounting policies opens the notes, followed by the detail behind line items, commitments and contingencies, fair-value disclosures, and subsequent events. Quarterly statements are condensed but must still disclose material changes since the annual report. Together these give the market a complete, comparable picture — the disclosure depth that distinguishes public reporting from a private company's leaner statements.

CMA bridge

This week ties FAR's EPS and segment rules, AUD's integrated-audit and CAM reporting, and REG's 1933/1934 Acts into the single public-reporting picture. For a closely held contractor like MBG the SOX and SEC requirements are not mandatory, but the same control discipline and the same EPS/segment mechanics are exactly what the exam tests across sections.

Practice and recap

  1. Match SEC forms to purpose: 10-K (annual/audited), 10-Q (quarterly/reviewed), 8-K (material events), S-1 (registration), Forms 3/4/5 (insiders).
  2. Compute diluted EPS with the treasury-stock and if-converted methods; include only dilutive securities.
  3. Apply segment (10% tests, 75% coverage, management approach) and interim (integral, estimated annual effective tax rate) reporting; disclose related parties, subsequent events, and risks.
  4. Reconcile non-GAAP measures (Reg G), tag in XBRL, and apply SOX §302/§404 certification and ICFR requirements.

Recap: public companies file the 10-K, 10-Q, and 8-K with MD&A and risk factors; diluted EPS adds dilutive options (treasury-stock method) and convertibles (if-converted) — $900,000 over 306,000 shares is $2.94; segment and interim rules plus related-party, subsequent-event, and risk disclosures inform investors; non-GAAP measures need a Reg G reconciliation; and Sarbanes-Oxley §302/§404 certification, ICFR, and the PCAOB underpin the reliability of it all.
